# Multi-Depot Vehicle Routing

Serve every customer from one of several depots, at minimum total travel cost, without exceeding
vehicle capacity. The multi-depot variant (MDVRP) adds a second, harder sub-problem on top of ordinary
routing: **which depot owns which customer**. Route order is a permutation problem; the depot
partition is an assignment problem, and they interact.

The instance of it built in [[optimization-methods]] makes three choices that move it away from the
textbook version and toward something that behaves like a real fleet.

## The three departures from the textbook

**1. Cost is directed road distance, not Euclidean.** Instances are built from real OpenStreetMap
drive networks via [[osmnx]], one-way streets respected, so `dist(a,b) ≠ dist(b,a)` in general. The
graph is truncated to its largest **strongly**-connected component so a shortest-path query never
meets an unreachable pair. Distances are resolved by [[lazy-dijkstra-distance-cache]] rather than a
precomputed matrix.

**2. Capacity is enforced per trip, and vehicles are multi-trip.** A vehicle serves, returns to its
depot, reloads, and goes out again. Total demand is engineered to be roughly 2–6× a single fleet
round, so the multi-trip behaviour is forced rather than incidental. Capacity is drawn per instance
from Uniform[40, 70] and is always greater than the maximum demand, so every customer fits in one
trip — that keeps infeasibility a property of the *plan*, not of the *instance*.

**3. The chromosome carries the partition explicitly.** Two aligned rows: a `sequence` permutation of
all customer ids, and a `depot_of` row assigning each customer a depot. Decoding groups by depot, then
greedily splits into capacity-feasible trips, then round-robins trips across that depot's vehicles.
Fitness is road distance plus `1e6 ×` overload units — infeasibility is priced, not forbidden.

The depot row is the load-bearing gene, and the repo learned that the hard way. It ships an
anti-regression assert because an earlier version silently destroyed the search:

> "A prior implementation shipped a sorted depot row, which silently collapses the assignment search;
> an anti-regression assert at population initialisation fails loudly if the depot gene ever comes out
> monotonic."
> — Optimization Methods/final_project/ARCHITECTURE.md, 2026-07-10

The {{operator-bake-off}} later confirmed the same thing quantitatively: only *Random* depot mutation
can re-partition, *Swap* merely permutes existing assignments, and every combination using Random beat
every combination using Swap.

## Instance scale

4 cities (`wroclaw berlin zurich budapest`) × 3 levels = 12 instances, 5000 m network radius,
per-city generation seeds 42–45.

| Level | Customers | Depots | Vehicles/depot |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| small | 50 | 2 | 1 |
| medium | 100 | 3 | 2 |
| large | 200 | 5 | 3 |

Demand per customer ~ Uniform[1, 20], drawn before capacity so that changing the capacity rule does
not resample the demands — a small determinism detail that makes instances comparable across reruns.

## The geography does not reproduce, and that is documented

Everything numeric is seeded and reproducible except the map itself:

> "Re-running the deterministic `greedy` on a freshly downloaded Wrocław graph gave 178,207 / 322,318
> / 458,921 m vs the paper's 177,555 / 299,944 / 481,089 m — same demands and capacity, but a
> different sampled road graph (OSM has drifted; today's largest SCC = 3,893 nodes)."
> — Optimization Methods/final_project/docs/DATA_VERIFICATION.md, 2026-07-09

The frozen paper artefacts (committed reports and chromosomes) are therefore the reference, not the
regenerated CSVs — which is why the instance and graph CSVs are gitignored and the reports are not.
See [[osmnx]] for the drift mechanism and [[generated-audit-artifact]] for how the check is published.
